params.question: A patient's corneal endothelial cell count has fallen to 480 cells/mm², and the cornea appears cloudy. Which mechanism of corneal transparency has primarily failed?

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Avascularity prevents blood vessels from entering the cornea but is not directly affected by endothelial cell loss. Corneal neovascularisation is typically triggered by chronic hypoxia, such as extended contact lens wear, not by pump failure.

answers.text: Regular collagen fibril spacing in the Maurice lattice

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The Maurice lattice describes the precise arrangement of Type I collagen fibrils that causes destructive interference of scattered light. While stromal oedema can secondarily disrupt this arrangement, the primary failure when endothelial cells are lost is the dehydration pump.

The endothelium's Na-K-ATPase pump actively removes water from the stroma, maintaining its water content at about 78%. When the cell count drops below approximately 500 cells/mm², this pump fails, water floods the stroma, and the cornea becomes oedematous — bullous keratopathy.

answers.text: Continuous epithelial renewal from limbal stem cells

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Limbal stem cell renewal maintains the surface epithelium but is independent of the endothelial cell count. Limbal stem cell deficiency causes a different set of problems, including persistent epithelial erosions and conjunctivalisation.

overallFeedback.feedback: The cornea has three transparency mechanisms: avascularity, regular collagen spacing, and the endothelial pump. With an endothelial cell count of 480 cells/mm² — well below the critical threshold of approximately 500 — the pump has failed, allowing water to flood the stroma and cloud the cornea.

Correct. The endothelial pump is the critical mechanism lost here. Remember that endothelial cells do not regenerate — every intraocular surgery risks further cell loss, making preoperative cell counts by specular microscopy essential.

params.question: A farmer presents 10 days after a paddy thorn injury. The corneal infiltrate is dry and grey-white with feathery margins, satellite lesions, and an endothelial plaque is visible. Which treatment is most appropriate?

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Fluoroquinolones treat bacterial keratitis, which presents with a dense, creamy-white infiltrate reaching maximum size within 24–48 hours. The subacute onset after vegetative trauma and feathery margins here point to a fungal, not bacterial, aetiology.

This is the classic presentation of fungal keratitis: subacute onset 5–14 days after vegetative trauma, dry grey-white infiltrate with feathery (hyphate) margins, satellite lesions, and an endothelial plaque. Natamycin 5% hourly is first-line treatment. Mistaking this for bacterial keratitis and prescribing antibiotics alone is the treatment mismatch that causes preventable corneal blindness in rural India.

Aciclovir treats herpes simplex keratitis, which presents as a branching dendritic ulcer with terminal bulbs and reduced corneal sensation — a very different pattern from the dry infiltrate with satellite lesions seen here.

PHMB with chlorhexidine treats Acanthamoeba keratitis, which is associated with contact lens wear and tap water exposure and presents with disproportionate pain, a ring infiltrate, and radial keratoneuritis — not the post-vegetative-trauma pattern described.

overallFeedback.feedback: This presentation — vegetative trauma, subacute onset (5–14 days), dry grey-white infiltrate with feathery margins, satellite lesions, and endothelial plaque — is classic fungal keratitis. Natamycin 5% hourly is the correct first-line treatment. Fungal keratitis is the commonest type of corneal ulcer in rural India.

Correct. The combination of vegetative trauma, subacute onset, feathery margins, and satellite lesions is the hallmark of fungal keratitis — the dominant type of corneal ulcer in rural India. Recognising this pattern prevents the devastating error of treating with antibiotics alone.

params.question: Following a healed corneal ulcer, a patient has a white corneal scar visible in direct light. On slit-lamp examination, the iris pattern is still partially discernible through the opacity. Which grade of corneal opacity does this represent?

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: A nebula is the faintest grade of corneal opacity, visible only on slit-lamp examination with the iris clearly seen through it. A white scar that is already visible in direct light is denser than a nebula.

A macula is moderately dense, visible in direct light, with the iris pattern still discernible through it. It sits between the faint nebula (slit-lamp only, iris clear) and the opaque leukoma (solid white, iris hidden) in the grading scale.
A leukoma is a solid white opacity through which the iris is completely hidden. Since the iris pattern is still partially visible in this case, the opacity has not reached leukoma grade.

An adherent leukoma is a specific entity where the iris has physically adhered to the posterior surface of the corneal scar, typically after corneal perforation. It is defined by iris adhesion, not merely by partial visibility of the iris through the scar.

overallFeedback.feedback: Corneal opacities are graded by density: nebula (faint, slit-lamp only, iris clearly visible), macula (moderate, visible in direct light, iris discernible), and leukoma (solid white, iris completely hidden). A white scar visible in direct light with a partially discernible iris is a macula.

Correct. The three grades of corneal opacity — nebula, macula, leukoma — are distinguished by density and iris visibility. Post-infective corneal scarring is the second leading cause of avoidable monocular blindness in India.

params.question: While assessing a metallic corneal foreign body at the slit lamp, you apply fluorescein under cobalt blue light and observe a green rivulet of fluid streaming from the wound. What is the most appropriate next step?

answers.text: Remove the foreign body immediately with a 23-gauge needle

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: A positive Seidel test confirms full-thickness corneal perforation with aqueous leaking from the anterior chamber. Attempting needle removal would risk expulsion of intraocular contents and worsen the injury.

answers.text: Instil proparacaine and schedule rust ring removal in 48 hours

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Rust ring removal is appropriate only for confirmed superficial foreign bodies where the Seidel test is negative. A perforated cornea requires urgent surgical intervention, not scheduled outpatient follow-up.

answers.text: Shield the eye without applying pressure and refer for urgent surgical repair

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: A positive Seidel test — a green rivulet of aqueous humour streaming from the wound under cobalt blue light — confirms corneal perforation. The correct action is to shield the eye (never a pressure patch, which could push intraocular contents out) and refer urgently for surgical repair.

answers.text: Prescribe topical antibiotics and arrange outpatient review in 48 hours

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: A corneal perforation is a surgical emergency. Outpatient management with antibiotics alone risks endophthalmitis, iris prolapse, and permanent vision loss.

overallFeedback.feedback: A green rivulet of fluid under cobalt blue light is a positive Seidel test, confirming full-thickness corneal perforation. The only correct action is to shield the eye without pressure and refer immediately for urgent surgical repair.

Correct. The Seidel test is the critical safety check before any corneal foreign body removal. A positive result — the green rivulet — means perforation. Shield and refer immediately; never attempt bedside removal of a perforating foreign body.
